domain: How radio-frequency triangulation locates a wildfire lookout's smoke sighting, and where the method breaks down in mountainous terrain
topic: How radio-frequency triangulation locates a wildfire lookout's smoke sighting, and where the method breaks down in mountainous terrain

source.title: Will We Ever Find Alien Civilizations?

movement.gist: Open at the widest level: the general problem of fixing a point in space from remote observation using only direction, no distance — the logic of triangulation as it applies across surveying, navigation, and astronomy, where two known points and two bearings determine a third unknown point.

Narrow to wildfire detection specifically: the fire-lookout network, the Osborne Firefinder alidade, the radio call-in of a single azimuth reading, and the practice of pairing lookouts so their bearings cross. Drop the thesis here as a passing remark — that triangulation's accuracy actually depends less on the instrument's precision than on what each lookout is aiming at.

Narrow further to a single case: two named lookout towers in a mountain district, their fixed stations and known separation distance, both radioing bearings on the same smoke plume on a specific afternoon.

Go inside the case: the ridge between the towers hides the fire's true base; each lookout is actually sighting a different visible portion of the drifting smoke column deflected by the ridge, not the fire itself, so their bearings intersect cleanly at a mathematically valid but physically empty point — the method fails not from measurement error but from both observers unknowingly aiming at different things while believing they aim at the same one. End on the small, practical fix crews actually use: cross-checking a lookout's reported bearing against known landmark bearings from that same tower before trusting the intersection at all.

tension_system.content_frame: The process: a fire lookout spots smoke, takes a compass bearing (an azimuth) to the plume using an Osborne Firefinder, and radios that single bearing to dispatch. Dispatch needs a second bearing from a different lookout station to triangulate the fire's position by finding where the two lines intersect on a map. The passage follows this from the abstract geometry of triangulation, down through the network of lookout towers, to one specific pair of stations, and finally into the failure mode: when the terrain between the two towers hides the fire's true base behind a ridge, both lookouts see the same visible smoke column but each is unknowingly sighting a different apparent source, so the two bearings intersect at a point where no fire exists.
